title: A Constitution for a Game
bigQuestion: Who gets to write the rules of a league, and whose voice is left out of the room?

story.title: The Windsor Hotel, November 1917
story.kicker: Hockey club owners in Montreal cannot vote one owner out, so they build a new league without him.
paragraphs: On November 26, 1917, men who ran professional hockey clubs met at the Windsor Hotel in Montreal. Canada was at war in Europe. The clubs belonged to the National Hockey Association, a league founded in 1909. Its owners had a problem they could not solve under their own rules.

The problem was Eddie Livingstone, who owned a Toronto club. The other owners had argued with him for years over players, money and schedules. The association's constitution gave them no simple way to push him out. Every owner was a member with rights under the league's own papers.

So the owners chose another path. They agreed to stop operating the old association and to form a new league. They called it the National Hockey League. Frank Calder, who had been the old league's secretary, became its president. Livingstone was not invited. The new league's Toronto team was run by the company that operated the Toronto arena.

No player sat at the table. Players signed with clubs, but the owners alone decided which clubs existed. Livingstone went to court and fought for years to win back what he had lost. The old association never played another game.

The National Hockey League played its first games in December 1917. More than a century later, it is one of the largest leagues in the world. It began with a lesson about governance: whoever writes a league's founding papers decides who belongs.
story.think: Why might owners start a whole new league instead of trying to remove one member under the old rules?

lessons.title: A Cricket Club Keeps the Laws
lessons.mainIdea: In England, private clubs such as the Marylebone Cricket Club became the keepers of a sport's written laws long before modern leagues existed.
reading: The oldest sports bodies in the English-speaking world were private *clubs*. A club was a group of members who paid dues and elected officers. The Jockey Club, formed at Newmarket around 1750, came to control horse racing in Britain. It set rules for races and settled disputes between owners.

The Marylebone Cricket Club, or MCC, was founded in London in 1787. It played at Lord's Cricket Ground. In 1788 the MCC issued its own revised Laws of Cricket. Other clubs across England began to follow them. Over time, the MCC became the accepted *custodian* of the laws, meaning the body trusted to keep and change them.

No one elected the MCC to this job. Its authority came from reputation and habit. Clubs chose to play by its laws because a shared code let them schedule matches. The MCC still holds the copyright to the Laws of Cricket today, even though the International Cricket Council now runs the world game.

words.d: a private group of members who pay dues, elect officers and agree on rules
the body trusted to keep a set of rules and decide how they change
the London club, founded in 1787, that became keeper of the Laws of Cricket

lessons.title: Thirteen Articles at Leith
lessons.mainIdea: Golf's oldest written rules came from an Edinburgh club in 1744, and two bodies, the R&A and the USGA, now share the job of keeping them.
reading: In 1744 the city of Edinburgh offered a silver club as a prize for a golf competition on the links at Leith. A group called the Gentlemen Golfers of Leith wrote thirteen *articles*, or numbered rules, for the event. Historians count them as the oldest known written rules of golf. The group later became the Honourable Company of Edinburgh Golfers.

Ten years later, in 1754, twenty-two noblemen and gentlemen formed the Society of St Andrews Golfers. They used rules much like those from Leith. In 1834 King William IV became the society's patron, and it took the name Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews. Over the next century, clubs around the world looked to St Andrews for rulings.

In the United States, five clubs founded the United States Golf Association, or *USGA*, in New York in December 1894. For decades the two bodies' rules differed in small ways. In 1952 they agreed on one shared code. In 2004 the St Andrews club handed its rule-making work to a separate organization called *The R&A*. Today The R&A and the USGA issue the Rules of Golf together.

the United States Golf Association, founded by five clubs in 1894
the body, separated from the St Andrews club in 2004, that keeps golf's rules with the USGA

lessons.title: A League Built to Remove an Owner
lessons.mainIdea: In 1917 hockey owners formed the National Hockey League so they could leave out one owner their old constitution would not let them expel.
reading: A *constitution* is an organization's founding document. It names the members, says how they vote and says how members can be removed. The National Hockey Association, founded in 1909, had such a document. Its members were clubs, and each club's owner held rights under it.

By 1917 most owners in the association wanted Toronto owner Eddie Livingstone gone. Their constitution made that hard. On November 26, 1917, they met in Montreal and formed the National Hockey League instead. Four clubs played its first season: the Montreal Canadiens, the Montreal Wanderers, the Ottawa Senators and a Toronto team. In January 1918 a fire destroyed the Wanderers' arena, and the club dropped out.

Livingstone sued the other owners. The court cases lasted for years, but he never got back into the league. Historians use the story to show a basic fact about leagues. A league is a *private association*, and its members can reshape it, or replace it, when enough of them agree.

words.d: an organization's founding document, naming its members, how they vote and how members can be removed
a group formed by private members under its own rules, not by the government
the hockey league formed in Montreal on November 26, 1917

lessons.title: Arena Owners Found a League
lessons.mainIdea: In 1946 owners of big arenas founded the Basketball Association of America to fill open dates, and it became half of the NBA in 1949.
reading: On June 6, 1946, a group of men met at the Commodore Hotel in New York City. Most of them owned or ran large indoor arenas in eastern and midwestern cities. Many of those arenas were built for hockey and ice shows. The owners wanted events to fill the nights when their buildings sat empty.

They founded the *Basketball Association of America*, or BAA. Its first president was Maurice Podoloff, a lawyer who also led the American Hockey League. The league's first game was played on November 1, 1946, at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto, between the Toronto Huskies and the New York Knickerbockers. Chicago had a team too, the Chicago Stags, which played from 1946 to 1950.

The BAA's founders were building owners first. That shaped the league's rules: teams belonged to arena companies, and schedules followed arena calendars. In 1949 the BAA joined with the older National Basketball League to form the National Basketball Association. The NBA still counts the 1946 founding as its own beginning. The *franchise*, a club's right to play in a league in a certain place, stayed the basic unit of membership.

words.d: the league founded by arena owners in New York in 1946, which became part of the NBA in 1949
a club's right, granted by its league, to play in a certain place
a large indoor building for sports and other events

lessons.title: Three Out of Four
lessons.mainIdea: League constitutions set high vote thresholds for the biggest decisions, which protects owners' shared interests and makes change slow.
reading: Not every league vote needs the same number of yes votes. A *simple majority* means more than half. A *supermajority* means a larger share, such as two-thirds or three-fourths. League constitutions save supermajorities for the choices that affect every owner's investment.

In the National Football League, approving a new owner or a team's move to a new city takes the votes of three-fourths of the clubs, which is 24 of the 32. Major League Baseball requires three-fourths of its clubs to approve a new controlling owner. The NBA's constitution lets its Board of Governors, made up of one representative from each team, end an owner's membership by a three-fourths vote.

These rules have a history. Each league began as a small group of owners who wanted to protect the value of their franchises. A high threshold makes it hard for a few owners to change the league. It also means that players, fans and cities are outside the vote, though they can push through bargaining, courts and public pressure.

a larger share of votes than a simple majority, such as three-fourths
the NBA's ruling body, with one representative from each team
the number of votes needed for a decision to pass

lessons.title: Two Stars Suspended, 1963
lessons.mainIdea: In 1963 NFL Commissioner Pete Rozelle suspended two star players for betting on games, showing how a commissioner uses the league's rules on gambling.
reading: Leagues have feared gambling since their early days. Baseball's owners created the office of *commissioner*, a single official with power over the whole sport, after a betting scandal around the 1919 World Series. Other leagues copied the idea. League constitutions often let the commissioner act against conduct *detrimental*, or harmful, to the league.

On April 17, 1963, NFL Commissioner Pete Rozelle suspended two stars indefinitely for betting on league games. They were Paul Hornung of the Green Bay Packers and Alex Karras of the Detroit Lions. Rozelle also fined five other Lions players for smaller bets. Neither was accused of trying to lose a game. The suspensions still kept both stars out for the full 1963 season.

Rozelle reinstated Hornung and Karras in March 1964. The rules they broke came from the league, not from criminal law. Gambling law later changed. In Murphy v. NCAA in 2018, the Supreme Court struck down a 1992 federal law that had kept most states from allowing sports betting. Illinois legalized sports betting in 2019, and leagues now write rules for a world where betting is legal.

words.d: a league official, hired by the owners, with power over the whole sport
harmful; leagues punish conduct detrimental to the league
a penalty that keeps a player or official out for a time
the 2018 Supreme Court case that let states allow sports betting

lessons.title: Pete Rose Signs an Agreement
lessons.mainIdea: In 1989 Pete Rose accepted permanent ineligibility from baseball, and the ban lasted until the commissioner ruled in 2025 that it ends at death.
reading: Pete Rose collected 4,256 hits, the most in major league history. In 1989 he was managing the Cincinnati Reds. Baseball hired lawyer John Dowd to investigate reports that Rose bet on games. The Dowd Report, delivered in May 1989, said Rose had bet on baseball, including on the Reds, while he was manager.

Rose sued, then settled. On August 24, 1989, Commissioner A. Bartlett Giamatti announced that Rose had agreed to be placed on baseball's *permanently ineligible list*. The agreement made no formal finding that Rose bet on baseball. At a news conference, Giamatti said he believed that Rose had. Giamatti died eight days later, on September 1, 1989.

In 1991 the National Baseball Hall of Fame, a separate private museum, voted that players on the ineligible list could not appear on its ballot. Rose denied betting on baseball for years, then admitted it in a 2004 book. He died in 2024. In May 2025 Commissioner Rob Manfred ruled that permanent ineligibility ends at death, and removed Rose and others, including Shoeless Joe Jackson, from the list.

the 1989 investigation that said Pete Rose bet on baseball
the private museum in Cooperstown, New York, that honors baseball players

lessons.title: An Owner Banned for Life, 2014
lessons.mainIdea: In 2014 the NBA used its constitution against an owner, banning Donald Sterling for life and moving to force the sale of his team.
reading: Rules against conduct usually point at players. In 2014 the NBA turned them on an owner. Donald Sterling had owned the Los Angeles Clippers since 1981. In April 2014, a recording was made public in which he made racist remarks about Black people. Players, sponsors and fans responded at once.

Adam Silver had become NBA commissioner on February 1, 2014. On April 29 he announced that Sterling was banned from the NBA for life. He also fined Sterling $2.5 million, the most the league's constitution allowed. Silver asked the Board of Governors to use its constitutional power to end Sterling's ownership. That required a three-fourths vote of the other owners.

The vote was never needed. Sterling's wife, Shelly Sterling, agreed to sell the team to Steve Ballmer, a former Microsoft chief executive, for $2 billion. Donald Sterling fought the sale in court and lost. The NBA approved the sale in August 2014. The case showed that a *lifetime ban* can reach the people who own the league, not only those who play in it.

lessons.title: Gentlemen and Players at Lord's
lessons.mainIdea: For more than 150 years English cricket split its players into amateur Gentlemen and paid Players, a divide the MCC ended in 1962.
reading: *Amateurism* is the belief that sport is best played for its own sake, without pay. Historians call it an *ideology*: a set of beliefs that seems natural to its holders but can serve some groups more than others. English cricket shows how the idea shaped daily life on the field.

From 1806, the MCC staged a match at Lord's between the Gentlemen, who were amateurs, and the Players, who were paid professionals. It became a yearly fixture for more than a century. At many grounds the two groups used separate dressing rooms and even separate gates to the field. Scorecards printed their names in different styles. Captains of England were almost always amateurs.

The line did not always match money. Some famous amateurs received large expense payments. Critics called this *shamateurism*, a mix of sham and amateurism. In 1952 Len Hutton became the first professional appointed to captain England in the 1900s. In November 1962 English cricket ended the distinction, and every player became simply a cricketer. The Gentlemen and Players match had been played for the last time that year.

lessons.title: Amateurs on State Payrolls
lessons.mainIdea: After the Soviet Union entered the Olympics in 1952, critics argued that state-supported athletes showed the amateur rule no longer matched reality.
reading: The Soviet Union first competed in the Summer Olympics at Helsinki in 1952. Its athletes were officially students, soldiers or workers. In practice, many trained full-time with support from the state, through army sports clubs and national programs. Other Eastern bloc countries built similar systems.

Western critics called these athletes *state amateurs*. Olympic rules barred athletes who were paid to compete. The Soviet athletes did not receive prize money or pro contracts, so they met the letter of the rule. Critics said they were full-time athletes all the same. Soviet and Eastern bloc critics answered that American college scholarships also paid athletes in another form.

Each side used the amateur ideal against the other during the *Cold War*, the contest for power between the United States and the Soviet Union from the late 1940s to 1991. The argument showed that amateurism could be defined in many ways. It helped wear down the rule. Over the following decades, Olympic sports opened step by step to athletes who were openly paid.

words.d: a critic's term for an athlete supported by the government while officially counted as an amateur
the contest for power between the United States and the Soviet Union from the late 1940s to 1991
the Soviet Union and the Communist states of Eastern Europe allied with it

lessons.title: Rugby Union Opens, 1995
lessons.mainIdea: In August 1995 rugby union's world body declared the sport open to professionals, ending a century of strict amateur rules.
reading: Rugby union's world body began in 1886 as the International Rugby Football Board. It is now called World Rugby. For more than a hundred years, it kept rugby union strictly amateur. Payments of almost any kind linked to the game could lead to a ban. Many who turned professional left for rugby league, a separate sport since 1895.

By the 1990s the rule was under strain. Top players spent more time training and touring than many full-time workers spent at their jobs. The 1995 Rugby World Cup in South Africa drew a large television audience. In June 1995 a media company owned by Rupert Murdoch agreed to fund new professional competitions for South Africa, New Zealand and Australia. A rival plan tried to sign the best players to a separate professional circuit.

On August 26, 1995, the board met in Paris and declared rugby union an *open game*. That meant players could now be paid. Clubs and national unions had to write contracts, salary rules and new structures in a hurry. The change came one hundred years after the 1895 split over paying players. The amateur ideal ended because its keepers voted it out.

the form of rugby governed by World Rugby, amateur until 1995
